local_calendar.t: Nevada holds its general election in November of each even-numbered year, and county, township, city, school district and general improvement district offices are filled at it, so those whose terms are ending are on the November 3, 2026 ballot. A nonpartisan office is missing from it when the June 9 primary settled it: a candidate with no opponent, or one who won a majority there, was declared elected (a judge of the district court in that position goes on to November alone). Irrigation districts hold their own elections in April.

local_coverage.t: Loaded for two of Nevada's seventeen counties, Clark and Washoe, each from its own election office's list of November contests and candidates: 125 contests and 208 names (county offices and constables; district court judges, justices of the peace and municipal court judges; city offices; school district trustees; water, improvement and other district boards). The other fifteen counties are not loaded yet. Not loaded from these lists: ballot questions, and the federal and state offices they also carry (Congress, the statewide offices, the Legislature, the Supreme Court and the Board of Regents). An office settled at the June primary is on neither list, because it is not on the November ballot.

measures.q: Should the Nevada Constitution be amended to create an individual’s fundamental right to an abortion, without interference by state or local governments, whenever the abortion is performed by a qualified healthcare professional until fetal viability or when necessary to protect the health or life of the pregnant individual at any point during the pregnancy?
measures.s:
EXPLANATION— This initiative, if approved by the voters, amends the Nevada Constitution to create a constitutional right to abortion.
This right to abortion would apply from the start of a person’s pregnancy up until the start of “fetal viability,” unless the pregnant person needs medical care to protect that person’s life or health, in which case the right applies throughout the pregnancy. “Fetal viability” means “the point in pregnancy when, in the professional judgment of the patient’s treating health care practitioner, there is a significant likelihood of the fetus’ sustained survival outside the uterus without the application of extraordinary medical measures.”
The initiative makes clear that the State of Nevada, including county and city governments in Nevada, generally cannot not interfere with this right. But a state, county, or city government can interfere with the right if there is a “compelling state interest” in doing so. A “compelling state interest” exists only if the government uses the least restrictive means to protect or improve the pregnant person’s life or health in ways that follow clinical standards of practice. Lastly, this proposed right to abortion does not require or force any individual in Nevada to have an abortion. Instead, it creates a right that allows an individual to make their own decision.
DIGEST—Existing law states that abortions are legal in Nevada and must occur within 24 weeks after the start of the pregnancy. An exception currently exists to allow an abortion after 24 weeks if a physician reasonably believes that an abortion is necessary to preserve the pregnant person’s life or health. Existing law also requires that abortions performed after the 24th week of pregnancy be performed in a hospital licensed by the State of Nevada.
If approved by the voters, this ballot measure would add a new section to Article 1 of the Nevada Constitution with the following information.
Section 1 of this amendment to the Nevada Constitution would create a “fundamental right to abortion.” This means that the Nevada Constitution would make abortion a legal option for all individuals, not just Nevadans, that is protected by the Nevada Constitution. The proposed amendment also includes the right to have an abortion procedure done by a qualified healthcare professional.
The amendment proposes that the right to an abortion would extend until “fetal viability, or when needed to protect the life or health of the pregnant patient.” “Fetal viability” means “the point in pregnancy when, in the professional judgment of the patient’s treating health care practitioner, there is a significant likelihood of the fetus’ sustained survival outside the uterus without the application of extraordinary medical measures.”
If the abortion would be necessary to protect the pregnant person’s life or health, the proposed amendment allows an abortion procedure to be carried out after the start of fetal viability.
The proposed amendment would also generally prevent the State of Nevada or any of its political subdivisions (e.g., the Nevada Legislature, county and city governments) from interfering with the constitutional right to abortion. State and local governments can interfere with this right only if they have a “compelling state interest” in doing so. A “compelling state interest” exists only if the government uses the least restrictive means to protect or improve the pregnant person’s life or health in ways that follow clinical standards of practice. Section 2 of the proposed constitutional amendment states that if any part of the amendment is challenged in court, then the rest of the amendment is not affected and remains in force. This section ensures that the right to abortion is protected to the greatest extent possible in the event of future lawsuits.
measures.sb: The explanation and digest printed with the question in the Clark County Election Department's sample ballot guide for the 2026 general election. The Secretary of State's 2026 ballot question guide, which carries the statewide text, could not be read.
measures.y: A “Yes” vote would create a new section of the Nevada Constitution to establish a person’s constitutional right to abortion, so that a person can make decisions about matters relating to abortion and reproductive healthcare, without interference from state or local governments.
measures.no: A “No” vote would keep the Nevada Constitution in its current form and would not impact the availability of abortion as a statutory right under Nevada law.
measures.f:
FINANCIAL IMPACT – CANNOT BE DETERMINED
OVERVIEW
The Statewide Constitutional Initiative Petition – Identifier: C-05-2023 (Initiative) proposes to amend Article 1 of the Nevada Constitution by adding a new section, designated as Section 25, establishing a fundamental right to abortion performed or administered by a qualified health care practitioner until fetal viability, or when needed to protect the life or health of the pregnant patient, without interference from the state or its political subdivisions, unless the denial of that right is justified by a compelling state interest that is achieved by the least restrictive means.
FINANCIAL IMPACT OF THE INITIATIVE
Pursuant to Article 19, Section 2 of the Nevada Constitution, an initiative proposing to amend the Nevada Constitution must be approved by the voters at two successive general elections in order to become a part of the Constitution. If this Initiative is approved by voters at the November 2024 and November 2026 General Elections, the provisions of the Initiative would become effective on the fourth Tuesday of November 2026 (November 24, 2026), when the votes are canvassed by the Supreme Court pursuant to NRS 293.395.
If this Initiative is approved by the voters at the November 2024 and November 2026 General Elections, the Legislature may be required to evaluate existing laws governing abortion to determine whether they are in compliance with the provisions of this amendment. If it is determined that existing laws are not in compliance, it is possible that the amount of resources utilized by the State or local governments for the administration or enforcement of new abortion laws that would comply with these provisions may be affected.
However, because it is unknown what laws, if any, may not be in compliance with the provisions of the Initiative, nor is it known how the Legislature may revise existing laws if they are determined to not comply with these provisions, the financial effect upon the State or local governments cannot be determined with any reasonable degree of certainty.
measures.fb: The Fiscal Analysis Division of the Legislative Counsel Bureau, dated August 1, 2024, as printed in the Clark County Election Department's guide.
measures.r: To become part of the constitution, an amendment proposed by initiative needs YES votes from a majority of the voters voting on it at two general elections in a row. This is the second of the two votes, so a majority YES now makes it part of the constitution once the Supreme Court canvasses the votes. (Nevada Constitution, article XIX, section 2, subsection 4)
measures.h: A citizen initiative, petition C-05-2023. An initiated amendment goes to the voters at two general elections in a row: approved at the first, in November 2024, it is now on the ballot a second time (Nevada Constitution, article XIX, section 2, subsection 4).

measures.q: Should the Nevada Constitution be amended to require voters to either present photo identification to verify their identity when voting in-person or to provide certain personal information to verify their identity when voting by mail ballot?
measures.s:
EXPLANATION— This initiative, if enacted, changes Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution to create a requirement for voters to provide identification before they receive a ballot. Voters who vote in-person at a polling place would need to show an ID that is current or that has not been expired for more than four years. If a voter is more than 70 years old, the identification could be expired for any length of time so long as it is otherwise valid. The acceptable forms of identification include:
1. Nevada driver’s license.
2. Identification card issued by the State of Nevada, any other State, or the US Government.
3. Employee photo identification card issued by the US government, Nevada government, or any county, municipality, board, authority, or other Nevada government entity.
4. US passport.
5. US military identification card.
6. Student photo identification card issued by a Nevada public college, university, or technical school.
7. Tribal photo identification.
8. Nevada concealed firearms permit.
9. Other form of government-issued photo identification that the Legislature may approve.
Voters who vote by mail ballot would need to include certain information so that election officials can use it to verify the voter’s identity. That information includes:
1. The last four digits of their Nevada driver’s license number.
2. If the voter does not possess a Nevada driver’s license, the last four digits of their Social Security number.
3. If the voter has neither a Nevada driver’s license or a Social Security number, the number provided by the county clerk when the voter registered to vote.
DIGEST— Under current law, Nevada voters must only show identification in certain situations. These situations are rare and related to the method and timing of how they register to vote. Currently only voters who register to vote by mail or computer, or who preregisters to vote by mail or computer, and who has not previously voted in an election for federal office in Nevada must provide identification. Additionally, state law requires voters who register to vote online less than 14 days before an election must also vote in-person and present an identification and proof of residency.
If approved by a vote by the voters during the 2024 general election it would go to the 2026 general election ballot for additional approval. If approved there, the Nevada Legislature could create related laws through legislation during the 2027 Legislative Session and these changes would go into effect for the 2028 election cycle.
measures.sb: The explanation and digest printed with the question in the Clark County Election Department's sample ballot guide for the 2026 general election. The Secretary of State's 2026 ballot question guide, which carries the statewide text, could not be read.
measures.y: A “Yes” vote would amend Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution to require in-person Nevada voters present certain identification and mail ballot voters to provide certain information in order to cast a legal ballot.
measures.no: A “No” vote would keep the Nevada Constitution in its current form.
measures.f:
FINANCIAL IMPACT – YES
OVERVIEW
The Statewide Constitutional Initiative Petition – Identifier: C-02-2023 (Initiative) proposes to amend Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution by adding new Sections 1B and 1C, as follows:
• Section 1B would require the presentation of a specified form of identification in order to vote in person in an election in Nevada, either through early voting or on election day.
• Section 1C would require voters who submit a mail-in ballot to provide certain specified information in order to verify that voter’s identity.
FINANCIAL IMPACT OF THE INITIATIVE
Pursuant to Article 19, Section 2 of the Nevada Constitution, an initiative proposing to amend the Nevada Constitution must be approved by the voters at two successive general elections in order to become a part of the Constitution. If this Initiative is approved by voters at the November 2024 and November 2026 General Elections, the provisions of the Initiative would become effective on the fourth Tuesday of November 2026 (November 24, 2026), when the votes are canvassed by the Supreme Court pursuant to NRS 293.395.
The provisions of the Initiative are anticipated to have a financial impact upon the State and local governments relating to procedures and systems utilized during the election process. The Secretary of State’s Office has indicated that these provisions will require modifications to processes and systems related to check-in of voters at the polling location and verification of mail-in ballots, as well as ensuring that the statewide voter registration system is modified to ensure that all data necessary to implement the provisions of the Initiative is captured. Based on information provided by the Secretary of State’s Office, the estimated costs to make these changes to voter systems in Nevada would be approximately $6,750, and these changes would need to be made in time for the elections that would be held in the year 2028. The provisions of the Initiative additionally allow the Legislature to determine additional forms of valid identification that can be used to verify identity for voting, aside from those already specified in the Initiative, which the Fiscal Analysis Division assumes will need to be created by the Legislature for those people who do not have or cannot obtain another form of allowable identification.
The Fiscal Analysis Division additionally assumes that this alternate form of voter identification will be provided to the voter at no cost, which means that the cost for these identification documents will be wholly borne by the State or by one or more local governments. However, the Initiative does not specify the form which these alternative identification documents must take, nor does it specify which agency or agencies (either at the state or local level) will be required to provide these documents. Additionally, it is unknown how many registered voters will not have one of the specified documents that would be acceptable to provide as proof of identity for in-person voting, who would need to be issued one of these alternative documents.
Thus, the financial effect upon the State or local governments relating to the issuance of an alternative identity document to those voters who will require such a document in order to vote in person cannot be determined with any reasonable degree of certainty.

measures.r: To become part of the constitution, an amendment proposed by initiative needs YES votes from a majority of the voters voting on it at two general elections in a row. This is the second of the two votes, so a majority YES now makes it part of the constitution once the Supreme Court canvasses the votes. (Nevada Constitution, article XIX, section 2, subsection 4)
measures.h: A citizen initiative, petition C-02-2023. An initiated amendment goes to the voters at two general elections in a row: approved at the first, in November 2024, it is now on the ballot a second time (Nevada Constitution, article XIX, section 2, subsection 4).

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from Nevada’s county boards of elections’ own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. Only the counties named below are loaded so far, so a race can be missing names from other counties. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read. From those lists this site reads only the office, the district, the county and the city, town or district a contest belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one. Addresses, phone numbers, e-mail and websites, where a list carries them, are never read, kept or shown. No photos, ages, biographies or campaign money are shown for state and local candidates.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Among the county and local contests here, cities, school districts and other districts are nonpartisan; county offices are some of each. Each contest’s own page says which, from the list it was read from.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
places

Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county or city it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the U.S. Census Bureau, the Clark County Election Department and the Washoe County Registrar of Voters, each named among these sources; where something on a county’s ballot could not be shown, that county’s page says what and why.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page and nothing more.
maps

Maps and “use my location”. District lines are the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary files), the lines the state pages draw, and the county lines are the Bureau’s too (2024 Census Bureau cartographic boundary file (counties, 1:500,000)); your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your district. Your location is worked out on your own device and never sent anywhere; a rounded copy (about half a mile) is kept on the device, with your choices, until you tap “Forget”. A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are counted only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Published polls by other pollsters that we have checked against their own release are shown apart, under Other published polls, for reference, and are never counted in the average; the rest are counted and named. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from the Census Bureau’s 119th Congress lines, the ones the Congress pages draw, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Top movers, and breaking-news alerts for Election Night
items: Top movers: a ticker on the Forecasts page, on Election Night's Forecasts page and on the front page shows the races whose forecast moved most since the previous day's, like a stock ticker: the state, the office, the leading candidate's chance and how many points it moved, and "now leads" where the lead changed hands. Each one opens the race's chart. It stops when you point at it or move to it with the keyboard, has a Pause button, and never moves for anyone who has Motion off, Calm on or reduced motion on their device: the races then sit in a row you can scroll. Labelled Analysis.

Election Night alerts: on the night (from 4 p.m. Central on November 3), a banner across the top of every page brings the news as it comes: polls closing in each state, each state's first official results, a race whose live forecast passes 95%, a new leader in the live forecast, and projections. An early projection comes when the model gives a candidate 99% or more with at least a quarter of the expected vote counted; a full projection, in a stronger brass band, from half counted. Each says how much is counted, is labelled Analysis and "as reported, not final", and the official count decides. A projection that stops holding is withdrawn in an alert of its own. Pause, See all alerts and Close are there; nothing makes a sound; before the night the pages ask for nothing.

changelog.title: Forecasts stamped with the date and time, newest polls, ballots cast
items: Every forecast now carries the date and time it was made, so you can follow how it moved. The forecast record keeps a copy each morning until November 2, and another whenever a new run of the model changes anything, each listed by the date and time it was taken; each race's small line follows its chance from one copy to the next.

Each race's chart marks the model's earlier runs with their date and time, placed by the hour on the time line. On the Forecasts page each race says when its forecast was made, and from the standard level up a small line shows how the leading candidate's chance moved, run by run; the top of the page says when the newest run was made.

Newest polls: new polls by members of the Transparency Initiative, each checked against the pollster's own release, add 19 race results to the averages: CNN's polls by SSRS in Kansas, Maine, Michigan and Texas (Senate and governor), Emerson in Kansas, ActiVote in Texas, East Carolina University in South Carolina, Concord in South Dakota and Montana, and High Point University in North Carolina (Senate and Supreme Court). 16 results by other pollsters, in Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, South Carolina and Texas, are shown apart and never averaged. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena polls of Minnesota and Florida, the Washington Post's of Kansas, Michigan State University's of Michigan) are listed as waiting, not shown. The poll finder no longer files a statewide poll under a House district.

Ballots cast so far: new counts from California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas. South Dakota's newest weekly file is held back: one of its own totals does not match its party rows, so its page keeps the October 23 figures until the state corrects it.
The forecasts were made again with the new polls and counts.

changelog.title: Sandbox: Reading & access, in lanes
items: A second sandbox experiment, on the draft site only: the reading and access settings sorted into six lanes (Language, How much, Text, Colour and contrast, Motion and calm, Ready-made sets). Open a lane and its settings are tabs: click one to pin it open, as many as you like, and your pins are kept on this device. Open another lane and it opens to the left of the first, so several can be open at once; on a phone they line up in a strip you swipe through.
The Language lane comes first and names every language with a finished translation in its own words. Choosing one shows the page again in that language, with the lane still open.
The settings are the site's own, so whatever is chosen there carries to every page. Every other page still opens the usual panel.

changelog.title: Final-week polls, Texas specials, Connecticut's towns, Election Night readiness
items: Final-week polls: 32 more polls, each checked against the pollster's own release. Polls by members of the Transparency Initiative count in the averages: Marquette, Marist, Siena, Michigan State, Concord, Emerson, Targoz, ActiVote and the University of North Florida, across Senate and governor races in Wisconsin, Maine, New York, Michigan, Nebraska, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Florida, and U.S. House districts NY-17, WA-03 and KY-06. Polls by others are shown apart and never averaged; those paid for by a campaign or a party say so. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena district polls, Emerson's subscriber-only district polls) are listed as waiting, not shown. The day's forecasts were made again with them.

Texas: the state's November 3 special elections for State House District 93 and State Senate District 22, the 276th District Court, a Democrat added to one judicial race, and nine declared write-ins are now on Texas's ballot pages, from the Secretary of State's own lists.

Connecticut: every town has now posted its sample ballot, and all are read: registrars of voters, town and school board contests, and every probate district now carry their candidates (110 local races, up from 76).

On state ballot pages, 43 kinds of local office that were listed at the end under their own titles (Florida's community development boards, library boards, receivers of taxes and others) now sit with the offices like them.

Election Night: Minnesota's saved results files are read about four times faster; Texas's two special elections and its judicial race are tied to the state's results; a new check holds back any state's file that shows votes before its polls close (three states' test files do today); and practice runs can no longer reach the public results.
Election Night counts 267 statewide races, and the U.S. page now names the District of Columbia's two offices apart from them. The Past results door now says all 50 states and DC are loaded.

State ballot pages: Georgia's and Virginia's mail-ballot notes no longer call October 23 "this Friday"; notes and source lines no longer describe how this site reads its files or show raw web addresses (each source's link is still there).

Wording: the news-outlet count now matches everywhere; the Method page says plainly that polls outside our average are shown apart; it says which Forecasts page lists every forecast; the privacy answers now name the Forecasts page's address look-up and street maps, and the Access page names the weather picture's one request; the page guide no longer says Minnesota is the only state with a forecast map.

changelog.title: A sandbox, and Anthropic's prospectus four ways
items: A sandbox on the draft site, for experiments: in no menu, not on the live site, and every page asks search engines not to list it.

Its first experiment is the prospectus Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026, four ways. As filed: a link to the official copy on SEC.gov. In chapters: save the official copy from SEC.gov and open it in a reader that rebuilds it into its 27 chapters, with highlights, notes, search, a page-by-page view as filed, and a PDF of a chapter, the chapters you marked, your notes alone or the whole filing. The copy and your notes stay on your device; this site never holds the filing's text. In five minutes: about 1,230 words in the filing's own order, in our words, checked claim by claim against the filing. And an analysis of whether it reads as if an AI wrote it: whether text carries a mark that says so (it does not, for anyone to read), and the word counts studies tie to AI writing, beside eight other prospectuses, four of them filed before ChatGPT existed. Every figure there is labelled Analysis and says what it cannot tell you.
The pages say the site is built with the help of Claude, and that Anthropic had no part in them.

Ballots cast so far: California, South Dakota, Colorado, Louisiana, Oregon and South Carolina are current again, read from the new names and layouts their offices now use. Iowa's site now refuses programs and Washington shows its counts only inside a dashboard, so both wait for a hand-saved copy; Oklahoma has not posted yet. Building these pages takes under a second, down from half an hour.

changelog.title: Every state on the forecast map
items: Each state on both Forecasts pages now has its map and "Your ballot, as forecast", with Share: all 40 states with a forecast, not Minnesota alone. Use your location or type your address, and the page lists every race on your ballot there with the model's forecast where it has one. Your location stays on your device.
A state's map and its list of races load only when you open that state.
In the states that drew new congressional lines for 2026, the map says so, and your U.S. House district is found only from the new lines, never the old ones.

The nine states with new U.S. House districts for 2026 (Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Utah) now show those districts on the ballot maps, from the Census Bureau's 2026 plan files published October 6, and "Use my location" or a typed address finds your 2026 district there. Before, those maps showed only the state's outline.

A statewide board elected by district (Texas's State Board of Education and others) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is placed by its own district, or the page says it cannot tell which seat is yours.
Past results load from the site's own results store rather than from each copy of the site, which leaves more room for election week.

Where a state's precinct lines are not on file here, your ballot still lists its statewide races. A statewide board elected by district (a state board of education, a public service commission) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is counted among the races the page could not place, and the state's own ballot lookup is the authority.

city_attorney.t: The city attorney is the city's lawyer. The office advises city leaders, drafts laws and contracts, defends the city in court and often brings cases for minor crimes.

North Carolina General Statutes 7A-272 (jurisdiction of district court), North Carolina General Assembly
Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Washington State Courts
Court System Information, Alaska Court System
The Judicial System, Local Government Handbook, New York Department of State

x.es: En la mayoría de estos estados, el tribunal de distrito es el principal tribunal de primera instancia, donde empiezan la mayoría de los casos. En Alabama, Michigan, Washington, Nueva York y algunos otros estados, es un tribunal inferior para delitos menores, casos de tránsito y demandas pequeñas.

governor.t: The governor is the state's top leader. The governor signs or vetoes new laws, names many state officials and leads the state's military forces.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 4 (Executive Department), Texas Legislature
Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article V (Executive Branch), Michigan Legislature

x.es: El gobernador es el líder principal del estado. El gobernador firma o veta las nuevas leyes, nombra a muchos funcionarios estatales y dirige las fuerzas militares del estado.

justice_of_the_peace.t: What a justice of the peace does depends on the state. In Texas, Louisiana and Montana it is a judge of a small local court, and in Vermont it means helping run elections and marrying couples.
s: Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Montana Judicial Branch
State and Local Government, Chapter 1 Part B: The Judicial Branch, Louisiana House of Representatives
Local Office Descriptions, Vermont Secretary of State

x.es: Lo que hace un juez de paz depende del estado. En Texas, Luisiana y Montana es el juez de un pequeño tribunal local, y en Vermont significa ayudar a administrar las elecciones y casar a parejas.

lieutenant_governor.t: The lieutenant governor steps in for the governor, and takes over if the job opens up. In many states this office also leads the state Senate.
s: Texas Constitution, Article 4 (Executive Department), Texas Legislature
Role of the Lt. Governor, Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Hawaii

x.es: El teniente gobernador sustituye al gobernador cuando es necesario, y asume el cargo si este queda vacante. En muchos estados, este cargo también dirige el Senado estatal.

mayor.t: The mayor is the city's elected leader and, in some cities, runs city departments. Where the council hires a city manager, the mayor leads the council and the manager does the daily work.
s: Kentucky Municipal Statutory Law, Informational Bulletin No. 145, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El alcalde es el líder elegido de la ciudad y, en algunas ciudades, dirige los departamentos municipales. Donde el concejo contrata a un administrador municipal, el alcalde dirige el concejo y el administrador hace el trabajo diario.

municipal_court.t: A municipal court is a city's own court. It handles broken city laws, traffic cases and minor crimes that happen in the city.
s: Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Washington State Courts
Municipal Courts - Function, Wisconsin Court System
Texas Courts: A Descriptive Summary, Texas Judicial Branch
Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Montana Judicial Branch

x.es: Un tribunal municipal es el tribunal propio de una ciudad. Atiende las violaciones de las leyes de la ciudad, los casos de tránsito y los delitos menores que ocurren en la ciudad.

public_administrator.t: When someone dies and no family member or executor can step in, the public administrator looks after their property. The office can settle the estate under a court's watch.
s: Administer Estate Under Direction of Probate Court, Clark County Public Administrator

x.es: Cuando alguien muere y ningún familiar ni albacea puede hacerse cargo, el administrador público cuida sus bienes. La oficina puede liquidar la herencia bajo la supervisión de un tribunal.

school_board.t: The school board runs a public school district. It hires the superintendent, sets district rules, passes the budget and, in many states, sets the local school tax.
s: Statutory Requirements for School Districts, Informational Paper 29 (Wisconsin Legislative Fiscal Bureau), Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction
Board of Education, Mercer County Schools, Kentucky
SBDM Councils & School Board Duties, Oldham County Schools, Kentucky

x.es: La junta escolar dirige un distrito escolar público. Contrata al superintendente, fija las reglas del distrito, aprueba el presupuesto y, en muchos estados, fija el impuesto escolar local.

secretary_of_state.t: In most states, the secretary of state runs elections and keeps records, such as business filings. Other duties differ by state.
s: Secretary of State Divisions & Programs, Nebraska Secretary of State

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el secretario de estado administra las elecciones y guarda registros, como los documentos que presentan las empresas. Las demás funciones varían según el estado.

state_controller.t: The state controller is the state's chief money officer. The office keeps the state's books, pays its bills and workers, and checks that money is spent as the law allows.
s: Duties of the State Controller, Idaho State Controller's Office
State Controller's Functions, California State Controller

x.es: El contralor estatal es el principal funcionario encargado del dinero del estado. La oficina lleva la contabilidad del estado, paga sus cuentas y a sus trabajadores, y verifica que el dinero se gaste como lo permite la ley.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Q&A, Colorado House of Representatives

x.es: La Cámara de Representantes del estado (llamada Asamblea o Cámara de Delegados en algunos estados) es la cámara más grande. Sus miembros redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.
s: What is the Legislature?, Wisconsin State Legislature
Legislative Branch Function and Process, North Dakota Legislative Branch

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

state_treasurer.t: The state treasurer keeps the state's money safe. The office takes in and invests state money, pays it out, and in many states returns lost money to its owners.
s: Illinois Constitution, Article V, Section 18 (Treasurer - duties), Illinois General Assembly

x.es: El tesorero estatal guarda de forma segura el dinero del estado. La oficina recibe e invierte el dinero del estado, hace los pagos y, en muchos estados, devuelve el dinero perdido a sus dueños.

town_advisory_board.t: In Clark County, Nevada, this board advises the county commission about a town outside any city. It acts as a link between the town's residents and the commission.
s: Town Advisory Boards/Citizens Advisory Councils, Clark County, Nevada

x.es: En el condado de Clark, Nevada, esta junta asesora a la comisión del condado sobre un pueblo que no forma parte de ninguna ciudad. Sirve de enlace entre los residentes del pueblo y la comisión.

water_board.t: Water district board members run a public district that supplies water, and in some places sewer service or farm water, to its area. They set its rates and budget.
s: What's So Special About Special Districts? (4th ed.), California Senate Local Government Committee

x.es: Los miembros de la junta de un distrito de suministro de agua dirigen un distrito público que suministra agua a su zona y, en algunos lugares, servicio de alcantarillado o agua para la agricultura. Fijan sus tarifas y su presupuesto.
